title: Equation builder
intro: Gauss's and Ampère's laws are always true, but they only hand you the field when the symmetry is right. This walks through the choices — symmetry, coordinate system, surface or loop, what the integral collapses to, what is enclosed — one decision at a time. Wrong turns are allowed; each one says why it doesn't work.

stepWords.shape: Which coordinate system and Gaussian surface?
Which coordinate system and Amperian loop?

spherical.name: Spherical
spherical.test: Every point at the same distance r from one center looks the same. Rotate the source any way about that center and nothing changes.

cylindrical.name: Cylindrical
cylindrical.test: Every point at the same distance ρ from one axis looks the same. Slide along the axis or rotate about it and nothing changes — which needs the source to be infinitely long.
cylindrical.direction: radial from the axis, $\hat{\mathbf{a}}_\rho$ (for E) — or circling it, $\hat{\mathbf{a}}_\phi$ (for B)

planar.name: Planar
planar.test: Every point at the same distance from one plane looks the same. Slide anywhere parallel to the plane and nothing changes — which needs the source to be infinite in extent.
planar.coords: Cartesian, with one axis normal to the plane
planar.direction: normal to the plane (for E) — or parallel to it, perpendicular to the current (for B)

none.name: Not enough symmetry
none.test: There is no family of points on which the field is guaranteed to have the same magnitude and a known direction. The law still holds; it just won't give you the field.

symmetryWrong.spherical>cylindrical: Cylindrical symmetry needs an axis you can slide along without anything changing. Pick any line through this source and move along it: your distance to the source changes. There is a center, not an axis.
symmetryWrong.spherical>planar: Planar symmetry needs a plane you can slide parallel to without anything changing. This source is localized; move sideways and the geometry changes. There is a center, not a plane.
symmetryWrong.cylindrical>spherical: Spherical symmetry needs a single center that every point relates to by distance alone. This source has an axis; two points at the same distance from the axis but different heights are equivalent, while two points at the same distance from any one center need not be.
symmetryWrong.cylindrical>planar: Planar symmetry needs an infinite flat source. This one is infinite in one direction (along the axis) but not in two — go around it and the geometry repeats, go sideways and it doesn't.
symmetryWrong.planar>spherical: Spherical symmetry needs a center. An infinite plane has none — every point on it is equivalent, so there is nothing to be the center.
symmetryWrong.planar>cylindrical: Close, but cylindrical symmetry picks out one axis. An infinite plane is symmetric under sliding in *two* directions and about *any* normal line — that is more symmetry than cylindrical, and it is called planar.
symmetryWrong.none>spherical: No. Spherical symmetry needs every direction from a center to look the same. This source does not — check whether rotating it about any center leaves it unchanged.
symmetryWrong.none>cylindrical: No. Cylindrical symmetry needs an infinite axis to slide along. This source is finite along any candidate axis (or has no axis at all), so the field at a given distance depends on where along it you are.
symmetryWrong.none>planar: No. Planar symmetry needs an infinite flat source. This one is localized.
symmetryWrong.any>none: There is enough symmetry here. Ask: what can I do to this source — rotate it, slide it — without changing it at all? Each such move is a symmetry, and together they fix the field's direction and what it can depend on.
symmetryWrong.B>spherical: No static magnetic field has spherical symmetry. B circulates around its source, and there is no way to assign a circulation direction at every point of a sphere consistently (the 'hairy ball' problem). That is also why ∮B·dS = 0 can never be used to find B.

sphere.name: Sphere of radius r, centered on the source
sphere.why: E is radial and |E| depends only on r, so on this sphere E is everywhere normal to the surface and constant in magnitude. The dot product is just |E| dS everywhere.

cylinder.name: Coaxial cylinder of radius ρ and length L, with flat end caps
cylinder.why: E points straight out from the axis and |E| depends only on ρ. On the curved side E is normal and constant; on the end caps E runs parallel to the surface, so E·dS = 0 there.

pillbox.name: Pillbox: a short cylinder with faces of area A parallel to the source, straddling it
pillbox.why: E is normal to the plane and the same magnitude on both faces (pointing away from each). Through the faces E·dS = |E| A; through the curved side E is parallel to the surface and contributes nothing.

cube.name: Cube centered on the source
cube.why: Gauss's law holds on a cube — the flux is still Q_enc/ε₀. But |E| varies across each face and E is not normal to the faces except at their centers, so you cannot pull |E| out of the integral. True, not useful.

circle.name: Circle of radius ρ centered on the axis, in a plane perpendicular to it
circle.why: B circles the axis and |B| depends only on ρ. Along this circle B is everywhere tangent to the path and constant in magnitude, so B·dl = |B| dl all the way round.

rectangle.name: Rectangle with one side of length ℓ parallel to the source, closed by sides perpendicular to it
rectangle.why: B runs parallel to the source and |B| depends only on the normal distance. Along the parallel side B·dl = |B| ℓ; along the perpendicular sides B ⊥ dl so they contribute nothing; the far parallel side is placed where B is known (zero, or equal and opposite).

circle-off.name: Circle not centered on the axis
circle-off.why: Ampère's law still holds — the circulation is still μ₀ I_enc — but B is no longer tangent to the loop everywhere and |B| varies along it. Nothing comes out of the integral. True, not useful.

square.name: Square loop around the source, in the plane perpendicular to it
square.why: The circulation is μ₀ I_enc, but B is tangent to the square only at four points and its magnitude changes along each side. You would be back to integrating Biot–Savart to evaluate the left side.

gauss.spherical>cylinder: A cylinder has an axis; this source has a center. On the curved side E (radial from the center) is not perpendicular to the surface except on one ring, and |E| changes with height. The integral does not collapse.
gauss.spherical>pillbox: A pillbox is for a flat source. Here E fans out in all directions, so across each face |E| and the angle to dS both change.
gauss.cylindrical>sphere: E points away from the axis, not from a point. On a sphere, E is normal to the surface only on the equator and |E| varies with latitude. Nothing can be pulled out.
gauss.cylindrical>pillbox: A pillbox faces are flat and parallel to a plane. The field here is radial from an axis — on a flat face |E| and the angle to dS vary with position.
gauss.planar>sphere: E is uniform and normal to the plane. On a sphere the angle between E and dS runs from 0° to 180°; the total flux is fine (Gauss's law is true!) but |E| doesn't factor out.
gauss.planar>cylinder: Only if the cylinder's axis is normal to the plane and you use its end caps — in which case it *is* the pillbox. A cylinder lying parallel to the plane has E crossing its curved side at every angle.

ampere.cylindrical>rectangle: A rectangle is for a planar source (or the straight interior of a solenoid). Around a wire B circles; it is tangent to a rectangle's sides at isolated points only.
ampere.planar>circle: B from an infinite sheet is uniform and parallel to the sheet; a circle around it has B tangent at only two points and |B| the same on both sides but in opposite directions. The circulation is right, but |B| does not factor out — use the rectangle.

gauss.wrong: That is the area of a sphere. Your surface is not a sphere.
That is the curved side of a cylinder. Your surface is not a cylinder — or you are not using one.
The end caps don't count: there E is parallel to the surface, so E·dS = 0 on them. Only the curved side carries flux.
Two faces of area A each — that is a pillbox straddling a sheet. Your surface is not a pillbox.
The pillbox has *two* faces, and flux leaves through both (E points away from the sheet on each side). Unless one face is inside a conductor where E = 0, count both.

ampere.wrong: That is the circumference of a circle. Your loop is not a circle.
Ampère's law is a *line* integral; there is no length L to multiply by. 2πρL is the area of a cylinder's side — that belongs to Gauss's law.
One side of length ℓ where B is parallel to the path — that is the rectangle loop. Your loop is not a rectangle.

Two parallel sides each contributing |B| ℓ — that is the rectangle straddling a current *sheet*, where B is equal and opposite on the two sides and both run with the loop. It is not right for a solenoid, where the outside side has B = 0.
The perpendicular sides never count — B ⊥ dl there — so at most two of the four sides contribute.

configs.name: Point charge Q
configs.symmetryWhy: Rotate a point about itself any way you like: nothing changes. So E can depend only on distance r and must point radially — any sideways component would single out a direction the source doesn't have.
configs.sanity: This is Coulomb's law — Gauss's law had better reproduce it. The r² in the area cancels the 1/r² in the field; that cancellation is why Gauss's law works at all.
configs.twinNote: No magnetic twin: there is no magnetic point charge, which is exactly what ∮B·dS = 0 says.

configs.name: Uniformly charged solid sphere, radius a, total charge Q
configs.symmetryWhy: The sphere looks the same from every direction about its center, so E is radial and depends only on r — inside the sphere as well as outside.

regions.label: inside, r < a
regions.note: Only the charge inside radius r counts; with uniform density that is the volume fraction r³/a³.

regions.label: outside, r > a
regions.note: From outside, a uniform sphere is indistinguishable from a point charge at its center.

configs.sanity: E grows linearly inside, peaks at the surface, then falls as 1/r². The two expressions agree at r = a — check that. Far away it must look like a point charge, and it does.
configs.twinNote: No magnetic twin — spherically symmetric static B does not exist.

configs.name: Thin spherical shell, radius a, total charge Q
configs.symmetryWhy: Same as any sphere centered on the origin: radial E, depending on r only.

regions.label: inside, r < a
regions.note: No charge is enclosed, and by symmetry E can only be radial with one magnitude — so that magnitude is zero. Every bit of the shell's field cancels inside.

configs.sanity: E = 0 inside a charged shell is the result students doubt most. It follows from symmetry plus Q_enc = 0 — no integration of Coulomb's law needed. A conducting sphere in equilibrium behaves the same way.

configs.name: Infinite line charge ρ_L
configs.symmetryWhy: Slide along the line, or rotate about it: nothing changes. So E can depend only on the distance ρ from the line, and must point straight away from it — a component along the line would single out one direction along it, and a φ-component would single out a sense of rotation.

regions.label: any ρ > 0
regions.note: The length L of your Gaussian cylinder appears on both sides and cancels — as it must, since you chose it.

configs.sanity: Falls as 1/ρ, not 1/ρ²: the charge is spread along a line, so the field weakens more slowly than for a point. The L cancelling is your check that the surface was chosen correctly.
configs.twinNote: The Ampère twin is the long straight wire: same cylinder/circle geometry, with B circling instead of E radiating.

configs.name: Infinite solid cylinder, radius a, uniform ρ_v
configs.symmetryWhy: Infinite along its axis and round about it, so E is radial from the axis and depends on ρ only.

regions.label: outside, ρ > a
regions.note: Outside, ρ_v π a² is the charge per unit length — so this is the line-charge result with ρ_L = ρ_v π a².

configs.sanity: Linear inside, 1/ρ outside, continuous at ρ = a. Compare with the solid sphere: same shape of curve, different powers.
configs.twinNote: The Ampère twin is a wire of radius a with uniform current density — same inside/outside structure.

configs.name: Coaxial cable: inner conductor radius a with +ρ_L, outer shell at radius b with −ρ_L
configs.symmetryWhy: Both conductors share the axis and are infinitely long, so the whole structure has cylindrical symmetry: radial E, depending on ρ only.

regions.label: inside the inner conductor, ρ < a
regions.note: A conductor in equilibrium carries its charge on its surface; nothing is enclosed.

regions.label: between, a < ρ < b
regions.note: Only the inner conductor is enclosed. This is where the cable's capacitance lives.

regions.label: outside, ρ > b
regions.note: Equal and opposite charges enclosed. The field is confined to the gap — the point of a coaxial cable.

configs.sanity: Field only between the conductors, 1/ρ there. Integrate E from a to b to get V, divide ρ_L by it, and you have the capacitance per unit length: 2πε₀ / ln(b/a).
configs.twinNote: The Ampère twin is the coax carrying current I out on the inner conductor and back on the shell — B is confined to the gap the same way.

configs.name: Infinite sheet of charge ρ_S
configs.symmetryWhy: Slide anywhere parallel to the sheet, rotate about any normal: nothing changes. So E can depend only on the distance from the sheet and must point straight away from it — on both sides, by the mirror symmetry.

regions.label: either side, any distance
regions.note: The area A cancels. The distance from the sheet does not appear: the field is uniform.

configs.sanity: Uniform, independent of distance — for an *infinite* sheet. A real finite sheet looks like this only close to it and far from its edges. Two such sheets with opposite charge give the parallel-plate capacitor: fields add between, cancel outside.
configs.twinNote: The Ampère twin is the infinite current sheet: uniform B parallel to the sheet, same pillbox→rectangle swap.

configs.name: Infinite slab of thickness d, uniform ρ_v, centered on x = 0
configs.symmetryWhy: Infinite in y and z, so planar symmetry: E along x only, depending on x only, and odd about the midplane (zero at x = 0).

regions.label: inside, |x| < d/2 (pillbox from −x to +x)
regions.note: Center the pillbox on the midplane so both faces see the same |E| by symmetry; the enclosed slab thickness is 2x.

regions.label: outside, |x| > d/2
regions.note: Outside, the slab looks like a sheet with ρ_S = ρ_v d.

configs.sanity: Linear inside, constant outside, continuous at the faces, zero at the center by symmetry. Same pattern as the solid sphere and cylinder, in planar form.
configs.twinNote: The Ampère twin would be a thick slab of uniform current density; the same inside/outside structure appears.

configs.name: Electric dipole: +Q and −Q a distance d apart
configs.symmetryWhy: There is an axis (the line joining the charges) and a mirror plane, but no family of points on which |E| is constant and the direction known. Rotate about the axis and nothing changes — but slide along it and everything does, and the field has both radial and axial components that vary differently.
configs.dead: Gauss's law is still true: any closed surface around *both* charges encloses zero and has zero net flux. But that tells you nothing about E at any point. Use superposition of two Coulomb fields, or compute V = (Q/4πε₀)(1/r₊ − 1/r₋) and take −∇V.
configs.twinNote: The magnetic dipole (a small current loop) has the same problem for Ampère's law.

configs.name: Finite line charge of length L
configs.symmetryWhy: Rotating about the line still works, but sliding along it does not — the ends break the symmetry. So E depends on position along the line as well as distance from it, and picks up a component along the line. A coaxial Gaussian cylinder no longer has E normal and constant on its side.
configs.dead: Gauss's law holds but doesn't collapse. Integrate Coulomb's law along the line: dE = ρ_L dz' / (4πε₀R²) with R the vector from each dz' to the field point, then integrate component by component. The infinite-line formula is the limit L → ∞ (or the field very close to the middle of a long line).
configs.twinNote: Same story for a finite straight wire segment in Ampère's law: use Biot–Savart.

configs.name: Long straight wire, radius a, total current I (uniform density)
configs.symmetryWhy: Infinite along its axis and round about it, so |B| depends only on ρ. Direction: B must circle the wire (right-hand rule) — a radial component would violate ∮B·dS = 0, and an axial one would single out a direction along the wire.

regions.label: inside, ρ < a
regions.note: Only the current inside radius ρ threads the loop: the area fraction ρ²/a² for uniform J.

regions.label: outside, ρ > a
regions.note: From outside, the wire's radius doesn't matter.

configs.sanity: Linear inside, 1/ρ outside, continuous at ρ = a — exactly the solid-cylinder Gauss result with E → B, ρ_v → J, ε₀ → 1/μ₀. The 1/ρ outside is the result Biot–Savart gives for an infinite wire after a much longer integral.
configs.twinNote: The Gauss twin is the infinite line charge (outside) or the solid charged cylinder (inside and out).

configs.name: Coaxial cable: current I out on the inner conductor (radius a), back on the shell (b < ρ < c)
configs.symmetryWhy: Cylindrical symmetry of the whole structure: B circles the axis with |B| a function of ρ only.

regions.label: in the gap, a < ρ < b
regions.note: This is where the cable's inductance per unit length lives.

regions.label: inside the shell, b < ρ < c
regions.note: The return current enclosed so far subtracts; by ρ = c it has cancelled the inner current entirely.

regions.label: outside, ρ > c
regions.note: No net current threads the loop. The field is confined to the cable — why coax doesn't radiate or pick up interference.

configs.sanity: Check continuity at a, b and c. Integrating B across the gap gives the flux per unit length, hence L' = (μ₀/2π) ln(b/a) — the twin of the coax capacitance formula.
configs.twinNote: The Gauss twin is the charged coaxial cable.

configs.name: Infinite sheet of surface current K
configs.symmetryWhy: Slide anywhere parallel to the sheet: nothing changes, so B depends only on the normal distance. Direction: B must be parallel to the sheet and perpendicular to K (right-hand rule around each strip of current), reversing across the sheet.

regions.label: either side, any distance
regions.note: Both parallel sides of the rectangle run with B (it reverses, and so does your direction of travel), so each contributes |B| ℓ: 2|B|ℓ = μ₀ K ℓ.

configs.sanity: Uniform, independent of distance — the magnetic version of the charged sheet's E = ρ_S/2ε₀. Two sheets with opposite K give a uniform field between and zero outside: the flat-solenoid picture.
configs.twinNote: The Gauss twin is the infinite sheet of charge.

collapseWrong.l: Both long sides count here. B is parallel to the sheet and reverses across it; so does your direction of travel around the loop, so B·dl has the same sign on both. Each contributes |B|ℓ: total 2|B|ℓ.

configs.name: Long solenoid, n turns per meter, current I
configs.symmetryWhy: Infinitely long and round: sliding along the axis or rotating about it changes nothing. For a tightly wound coil the current is effectively a cylindrical sheet, so B is along the axis, depends on ρ at most — and a second argument (or ∮B·dS = 0 plus the field at infinity) shows it is uniform inside and zero outside.

regions.label: inside
regions.note: Rectangle with one side of length ℓ inside (B ∥ dl), the opposite side outside (B = 0), and two perpendicular sides (B ⊥ dl). It encloses nℓ turns.

regions.label: outside (ideal, infinite)
regions.note: A rectangle entirely outside encloses no current, and B must be uniform there too — so with B → 0 at infinity it is zero everywhere outside.

configs.sanity: Uniform inside, independent of radius and of where you are along the axis; zero outside. Real solenoids leak at the ends. Flux linkage per unit length gives L' = μ₀ n² (area).
configs.twinNote: No clean Gauss twin — there is no electric configuration with a uniform field confined inside a cylinder, since E lines must end on charge.

shapeWrong.circle: Inside an ideal solenoid B is uniform and along the axis. A circle in the cross-section has B perpendicular to dl everywhere: circulation zero, no current enclosed, consistent — and no information. Use a rectangle with one side inside, one outside.

collapseWrong.2pirho: A circle in the cross-section has B perpendicular to dl everywhere — zero circulation, nothing enclosed, no information. The loop that works is the rectangle with one side inside.

configs.name: Toroid, N turns total, current I
configs.symmetryWhy: Rotate about the toroid's central axis: nothing changes. B circles that axis inside the windings; |B| depends on ρ (and, strictly, on position in the cross-section — for a thin toroid that is negligible).

regions.label: inside the windings
regions.note: A circle of radius ρ inside the core threads all N turns once each.

regions.label: outside the windings (inside the hole, or beyond)
regions.note: In the hole no turns are threaded; beyond the outer edge each turn is threaded once going up and once coming down.

configs.sanity: Compare with the solenoid: N/(2πρ) is the turns per unit length along the circle, so this is μ₀ n I with n varying slightly across the core. Field confined to the core — why toroidal transformers are quiet.

shapeWrong.rectangle: Inside a toroid B circles the toroid's axis; a rectangle in the cross-section has B perpendicular to dl. Use a circle concentric with the toroid.

configs.name: Finite straight wire segment
configs.symmetryWhy: The ends break the slide-along symmetry, so |B| on a circle around the wire depends on where along the wire the circle sits. Worse: a finite segment alone isn't a steady current — charge would pile up at the ends. Ampère's law as written assumes closed circuits.
configs.dead: Use Biot–Savart: dB = μ₀ I dl × â_R / (4πR²), integrated along the segment. The infinite-wire result μ₀I/2πρ is the limit of a long segment seen from near its middle.
configs.twinNote: Same as the finite line charge for Gauss's law.

configs.name: Single circular current loop
configs.symmetryWhy: Rotating about the loop's axis works, but nothing else does. On any circle you might draw, B is not tangent with constant magnitude. The loop is the magnetic dipole — the twin of the electric dipole, which defeats Gauss's law the same way.
configs.dead: Ampère's law is true for every loop you draw, and useless for finding B. Biot–Savart gives the on-axis field in closed form, B = μ₀ I a² / (2(a² + z²)^{3/2}), and the far field is the dipole field.
configs.twinNote: The Gauss twin is the electric dipole.
